topic.title: Graph Learning with Limited Labels and Unknown Classes
topic.overview: Graph learners combine node features, connections, and scarce labels to predict or classify relational data. This cluster studies contrastive objectives, learned graph structure, semi-supervision, and distribution differences across graphs. Recent open-world methods also confront unlabeled nodes that belong to classes absent from training.
topic.whyItMatters: Message passing can spread useful supervision, but it can also propagate misleading relationships or assume every node belongs to a known category. A reliable learner must decide both what information to share and when the current label vocabulary is incomplete.
topic.evolution: Earlier representatives develop network metrics and inductive graph representations. Later work scales contrastive learning and handles federated or non-IID graphs. Recent methods reshape connectivity to improve label influence and combine textual semantics with topology to reject, annotate, and incorporate previously unknown classes.
openQuestions: How can learned graph edits be validated when labels are scarce?
What prevents automatic unknown-class annotation from reinforcing its own mistakes?

papers.title: Supervised Graph Contrastive Learning for Gene Regulatory Networks
papers.tldr: SupGCL uses real gene knockdown perturbations to supervise graph representations, improving disease structure and downstream predictions.

papers.title: When LLMs Encounter Open-world Graph Learning: A Fresh View on Unlabeled Data Uncertainty
papers.tldr: OGA combines text and graph structure to identify unknown-class nodes, annotate them, and incorporate unlabeled data into training.
